signs.fun_fact: The mouth sign is one of the most frequent hieroglyphs. As a logogram it means 'mouth' (rꜣ); as a phonogram it gives 'r'.
Two raised arms represent the 'ka' — one's spiritual double or life force. The ka was fed through offerings placed in tombs.

signs.fun_fact: The forearm was used in offering scenes — Egyptians extended the arm to present gifts to the gods. As a sign, it represents 'a' (ayin).
The hand gives 'd'. Egyptian artists always drew the hand with visible fingers, making this one of the most recognizable body-part signs.
Walking legs appear at the end of words related to movement. This is a determinative — a silent 'category tag' that helps readers understand meaning.
The foot/leg sign gives 'b'. Walking was the primary means of travel for most Egyptians — only royals and officials rode in chariots.

signs.fun_fact: Animal belly gives the sound 'X' (soft 'kh'). Butchery was depicted in almost every tomb — meat offerings were essential for the afterlife.
The heart was considered the seat of intelligence and emotion in ancient Egypt — not the brain, which was discarded during mummification.
The heart-and-windpipe gives 'nfr' meaning 'beautiful, good, perfect'. The word 'Nefertiti' comes from this — 'the beautiful one has come'.

signs.fun_fact: The ostrich feather represents Maat — truth, justice, and cosmic order. In the afterlife, your heart was weighed against this feather.
The horned viper was feared and respected. Despite being dangerous, its image became one of the alphabet's essential sounds: 'f'.
The cobra in repose gives the sound 'D' (like 'j' in 'jump'). The uraeus cobra on the pharaoh's crown was a symbol of royal authority.

The palm rib gives the triliteral 'rnp' and means 'year'. Egyptians notched palm ribs to count years — a living tally stick.

signs.fun_fact: The hillside slope gives the sound 'q'. Egypt's landscape alternated between flat floodplains and the desert hills that bordered the Nile valley.
Water ripples appear everywhere in Egyptian writing. The Nile was the source of all life, so it's fitting that its symbol became one of the most common sounds.
A pool of water gives the sound 'S' (like 'sh'). Ornamental pools were features of wealthy Egyptian gardens.
The house plan gives the sound 'pr'. Egyptian houses were built of mudbrick, and this bird's-eye view floor plan was the standard representation.
